events.text: The Heavenly Court is a hall so long that its far end is weather. Clerks sit at desks of cloud in rows that go out of sight, each copying the fates of the world below in a hand nobody will ever praise. An archivist with ink on his nose shows you to your desk. "Seol Haneul," he says. "Don't drink the ink. Everyone tries once."

effects.log: Seol Haneul laughs too. You have a friend in heaven, which is rarer than gods would admit.

choices.text: Sit down and begin at once

effects.log: You copy a hundred fates before the bell. Seol Haneul looks impressed and slightly worried.

choices.text: Ask who wrote the first fate

effects.log: "Nobody knows," Seol Haneul says. "That is the first thing they teach you not to ask."

events.text: A year of fates: a fisherman's good catch, a scholar's failed examination, a child's fever that breaks on the third night. You copy each one exactly, and each one, for a moment, is the whole world.

effects.log: You take a long time over the fever breaking. It is the only kindness a clerk may give.
You finish first in your row. The clerk beside you sighs with envy.

events.text: The Book of Fates has no index. Old Judge Dobu, passing your desk, tells you it never had one: "If you could look a fate up," the judge says, "someone would." Then the judge looks at your page for a long time and walks on.

choices.text: Ask the judge what that meant

effects.log: Judge Dobu only says: "Keep your hand steady and your eyes open."
You keep your hand steady. Your eyes, you keep open.

events.text: In the middle of a page, a line in another hand: a merchant's fate of ruin written over with a fate of fortune, the ink still faintly wet. Someone in the court has been selling fates, and has been careless with this one.

choices.text: Report it to the Jade Secretariat

effects.log: Minister Baek Ryeon's people take the page away. The minister sends a note of thanks in a beautiful hand.
You write the merchant's true fate back in. Nobody saw. You hope nobody saw.
You turn the page. The merchant will be rich. Somebody else, somewhere, will not.

events.text: A second forged line, in the same careless hand, and this time you know the hand: it is the writing on the Thunder Ministry's requisitions. Somebody very high up is selling the fates of mortals.

choices.text: Report it, and name the ministry

effects.log: The page goes to the Jade Secretariat. The Thunder Ministry, they say, has started asking about you.

choices.text: Fix the line and keep the secret

effects.log: You fix it. You keep the secret. It is a heavy thing to keep in heaven.

events.text: A soldier's soul stands before you: he followed orders, all his life, and some of the orders were evil. He does not ask for mercy. He asks you which orders he should have refused.

choices.text: Judge him by what he did

effects.log: You weigh each deed. The scale settles slowly. He bows to the verdict.

choices.text: Judge him by what he was told

effects.log: You lighten his sentence. Somewhere, a commander's scale grows heavier.

choices.text: Judge him as a warning to others

effects.log: The court approves of the harshness. You do not sleep well.

events.text: A thief's soul, a woman who stole bread for forty years for an orphanage nobody else would feed. The ledger is long and every line of it is a theft. The orphans' ledger, beside it, is longer.

effects.log: You weigh them both, line by line. It takes a month. It is fair.
The court frowns. The orphans' ledger, somehow, seems to glow.
You sentence her by the law. She thanks you, which is the worst part.

events.text: A rich man's soul arrives with gifts: jade, silk, a list of temples he built. He has the polished smile of a man who has never been judged by anyone he could not buy.

choices.text: Send the gifts back and read the ledger

effects.log: The ledger is less polished than the smile. Justice is done.

choices.text: Be gentle; he did build the temples

effects.log: The temples were real. So were the debts. You split the difference.
The court gossips about your severity for a year.

events.text: Two souls who died on the same day, in the same duel, each accusing the other. Both ledgers say the same thing in different words. Both are telling the truth as they remember it.

effects.log: You sentence them to the same rebirth, as neighbours. Judge Dobu laughs out loud when he hears.
They leave the hall still arguing. Some things heaven cannot fix.
Neither of them will duel again for a thousand years.

events.text: A healer's soul whose ledger is almost perfect, but for one patient lost to a moment of pride. The healer has come before you asking not to be forgiven for it.

effects.log: You judge the one moment as it was. The healer weeps with relief.
"You have no right," the healer says, and you see you were wrong.
It is what the healer asked for. It is still a hard verdict to give.

events.text: A village's whole ledger, brought in by mistake: three hundred souls of a place swept away in one flood. The clerks want them judged in one verdict, to clear the shelves.

effects.log: It takes a year. Each of them had a name. Each of them is heard.

choices.text: Pass them all to a gentle rebirth

effects.log: The clerks are glad. The village will be reborn as a village, somewhere dry.

choices.text: One verdict, as the clerks ask

effects.log: The shelves are cleared. You feel the weight of three hundred names you did not read.

events.text: The ledger is laid before you, and the name at the top is {echo_name}. You know the name the way one knows an old scar. The last line reads: {echo_cause}, at {echo_age}. Every deed of that life is written below it, and some of them you are not proud of.

choices.text: Judge it like any other soul

effects.log: You judge your own past life by the law, line by line. It is the hardest verdict you have ever given, and the fairest.
You soften every line. The scale tips. A clerk in the gallery writes something down.
You hand the ledger to Judge Dobu. "Good," the old judge says quietly. "That was the test."

events.text: The ledger of {echo_name} lies open before you, and beside it, by the court's custom, the ledger of the one who ended that life: {echo_killer}. Both souls are yours to judge today. One of them was you.

choices.text: Judge both by the law alone

effects.log: You give both verdicts as the law asks. Neither is what your old life would have wanted. Both are right.

choices.text: Spare the life you lived, and punish the one who ended it

effects.log: Revenge, a lifetime late, written in heaven's own ink. The gallery murmurs.
Judge Dobu takes them both. "Some debts," the old judge says, "are better paid by strangers."

events.text: {echo_name}'s soul does not stand before you; a soul cannot stand twice. Only the ledger comes, and a note from the clerk who found it: THIS ONE ASKED, BEFORE REBIRTH, TO BE JUDGED BY WHOEVER IT BECAME.

effects.log: You judge it. When you close the ledger, something old in you finally rests.
You write FORGIVEN across the page. It is not the law. It may be something better, or worse.

events.text: Something comes up the Southern Gate's stair from the world below: an old grievance of the earth given claws, made of every curse a mortal ever threw at heaven. You hold the gate. It does not pass.

effects.log: The stair is quiet again. Heaven goes on not noticing, as heaven does.

choices.text: Listen to the curses before they fade

effects.log: Most of them are about rain. Some of them are about you, specifically.

events.text: A delegation of foreign gods arrives at the Southern Gate without an invitation and with a great deal of thunder. You keep them waiting precisely as long as protocol allows, then let them in precisely as far as it allows.

choices.text: Bow exactly as low as they do

effects.log: The foreign gods are offended in a way that cannot be complained about. The court is delighted.

choices.text: Bow a little lower, as a kindness

effects.log: The eldest of them remembers it. Heaven's doors open a little wider for you later.

events.text: The thing on the stair is stronger than the gate's records said. It throws you against the doors and is through before you are up. The guards of the inner court stop it, eventually, and file a report with your name on it.

effects.log: You sign it. Marshal Cheon Mu's people read it with interest.

choices.text: Train at the gate all night

effects.log: Next time it will not get past. You make sure of it, bruise by bruise.

events.text: Heaven's host marches out under your banner: a hundred thousand spears of light against a rebellion of mountain spirits who have decided they are gods. By evening they have decided otherwise.

effects.log: They go back to being mountains, gratefully. The court calls it soft. The mountains call it wise.

choices.text: Bring their banners to the Jade Throne

effects.log: The banners are hung in the hall. Your name is read out after them.

events.text: A war in the clouds between two pantheons, and the court sends you to stop it. You stand between the armies with your banner and say, very loudly, that the next god to strike will answer to heaven. Nobody strikes.

choices.text: Hold the line until both armies leave

effects.log: It takes three days. They leave muttering, and alive.
Dinner is awkward, long, and the beginning of a treaty.

events.text: The rebellion was larger than the reports said, and your host comes back with half its banners. Nobody died who can die; gods do not, quite. But the hall is quiet when you report, and Marshal Cheon Mu does not look up.

effects.log: You take it. Some of the generals respect you for it. The marshal is not one of them.
The reports were wrong. It does not matter. The court remembers losses, not reasons.

events.text: Minister Baek Ryeon of the Jade Secretariat is a god of quiet voices and long sleeves, who has never once raised either. "Heaven runs on law," the minister tells you over tea. "Thunder only runs on itself."

effects.log: The minister refills your cup, which in the Secretariat is a sort of oath.
The minister notices you wondering, and likes you more for it.

events.text: Marshal Cheon Mu of the Thunder Ministry eats standing up and settles arguments by ending them. "The Secretariat writes laws," the marshal says, "and we make the world obey them. Which of us do you think heaven needs more?"

effects.log: The marshal laughs like a landslide. "A politician. Good. We need those too."
The marshal claps you on the back hard enough to crack a lesser god.

events.text: You spend the year belonging to nobody: bowing to the Secretariat, saluting the Ministry, and having very long conversations about the weather. Seol Haneul says it is the hardest work in heaven.

choices.text: Buy Seol Haneul a cup of cloud-wine

effects.log: He drinks it and says you would make a fine minister. Then he says he meant it as an insult.
Nobody quite knows what you think. In the court, that is a kind of armour.

events.text: Your brush touches one line of the Book of Fates, and below the clouds a fever breaks early, a debt is forgiven, a harvest comes in good. The ones you love will never know why their year turned. That is how it should be.

choices.text: Watch them from the edge of the clouds

effects.log: You watch for an hour. They are laughing about something. That is enough.
You burn it. It is not evidence, exactly. It is just safer.

events.text: You write one line into the fate of someone who wronged you, long ago, below. It is a small line. It will take them years to notice what it took. Your hand is steady. Your heart is not.

effects.log: It is still there. It will always be there now.

choices.text: Close the Book and walk away

effects.log: You walk a long way through the cloud halls before your heart slows.

events.text: Judge Dobu hands you a judge's seal with both hands, as if it were heavy. "It is," the old judge says, seeing your face. "It gets heavier. Every soul you judge stays in it."

choices.text: Take the seal with both hands too

effects.log: The judge nods. "Good. Never one hand."

choices.text: Ask how the judge has carried it so long

effects.log: "Badly," Judge Dobu says, and smiles for the first time.

events.text: The keys of the Southern Gate are not keys: they are a single word, whispered to you by the last gatekeeper as she lays down the post. She tells you never to say it aloud. Then she walks out of heaven without looking back.

effects.log: You keep it. It sits in your mouth like a cold stone, and every gate in heaven knows your step.
"Below," she says. "I want to see a sunrise from underneath."

events.text: The banner of heaven's host is unrolled at your feet, and the whole court rises. A hundred thousand spears of light salute. Somewhere in the back rows, a clerk with ink on his nose is cheering louder than anyone.

effects.log: Every god in the hall turns to see who you saluted. Seol Haneul turns very red.
The throne, which never answers, seems to answer.

events.text: Seol Haneul invites you to the archive after hours, where the oldest fates are kept in jars like pickled plums. "This one is the first sunrise," he whispers, lifting a jar. "Don't tell anyone I showed you."

effects.log: He grins. You are, it seems, the only friend he has in heaven.

choices.text: Tell him he will get caught

effects.log: "Probably," he says, putting the jar back. "Everyone does, eventually. Even you."

events.text: Seol Haneul is waiting at your desk with two cups of cloud-wine and a worried face. "The Thunder Ministry has been asking about your ledgers," he says. "I told them you were boring. Be boring for a while, please."

effects.log: "Don't thank me," he says. "Be boring." You try.

choices.text: Ask what he told them exactly

effects.log: He tells you, word for word. He is a very good friend and a very bad liar.

events.text: Seol Haneul passes your desk without a word, as he has for years now. Once, on a quiet evening, you catch him reading one of your old ledgers, very carefully, as if looking for something.

choices.text: Ask him what he is looking for

effects.log: "Nothing," he says, and closes it. "Nothing at all."
He reads until the lamps go out. You never learn what he found.

events.text: The accusation is read out in the hall where every god can hear it: a fate in the Book, rewritten in your hand. The Jade Secretariat looks at its sleeves. The Thunder Ministry looks at you. Seol Haneul, in the gallery, looks as if he might be sick.

effects.log: You listen to every word. The court will want your answer.
Seol Haneul meets your eyes, and nods, once.

events.text: You confess, plainly, and the court is so surprised by plainness that it forgets to be cruel. A rank is taken from you. You are allowed to keep your desk, your seal and, it turns out, your friends.

choices.text: Go back to work the same day

effects.log: The clerks watch you sit down. Some of them, quietly, respect it.

choices.text: Thank Judge Dobu for the sentence

effects.log: "Thank yourself," the old judge says. "Most of them lie."

events.text: Your patron rises and speaks, and the charge is dropped as if it had never been more than a rumour. Nobody looks at you as they leave. Everyone will remember.

effects.log: Your patron says there is no need. You both know there will be a need, one day.
The cloud halls are very long when everyone is watching you walk.

events.text: The court finds against you. Your seal is broken in front of the hall, and its pieces are swept up by a clerk who will not meet your eyes. You are a god still. You are no longer heaven's servant.

choices.text: Bow to the court and go

effects.log: You bow. Some of the old gods bow back, which they did not have to do.

choices.text: Say what you think of the court

effects.log: You say it. It is recorded. It is, some say later, the best speech the hall ever heard.

events.text: You say the hand was Seol Haneul's. He does not argue. He looks at you once, a long look, and lets them put the chains of light on him. You keep your rank. You keep everything.

effects.log: You look away. You will be looking away from this for a very long time.
You watch him all the way out of the hall. He does not look back again.

events.text: A young clerk of the Heavenly Court stops you in the cloud halls and bows very low. "Forgive me," the clerk says. "The archive has a portrait of a General of Heaven with your soul's light. We were told one day you would come back."

effects.log: The portrait has a different face. The eyes are yours.

choices.text: Tell the clerk to stop bowing

effects.log: The clerk stops, and starts again, and gives up, and laughs.

events.text: At the Southern Gate a guard checks a long scroll, frowns, and checks it again. "Your soul's light is on the list of the cast out," the guard says, "from long ago. It says you may enter. It says to watch you."

effects.log: The guard does not smile back. Heaven has a long memory and no sense of humour.
The guard reads it out: "Bent a fate." Then, more quietly: "My grandmother said that was not always wrong."
